subject: The Fourth Amendment 'automobile exception' — Carroll v. United States (1925) and the bright line drawn in Collins v. Virginia (2018)
central_question: Can the police search your car without a warrant — and where, exactly, is the line they still cannot cross?
viewer_promise: By the end, the viewer understands why police have been allowed to search a car without a warrant for a hundred years, what actually triggers that power (probable cause, not a hunch), and the one place — the ground right next to your home — where even your car is still protected.
surprise: Most people assume a search of their car needs a warrant. It usually doesn't: a 1925 case built a permanent 'automobile exception,' and it has quietly governed roadside searches ever since — until a 2018 case about a motorcycle under a tarp in a driveway drew the line the Court would not let police cross.
stakes: Whether an officer can open your trunk, your glovebox, and the bags inside your car on the roadside without a warrant; what 'probable cause' really requires; and how the Court balances the mobility of a car against the sanctity of the home's immediate surroundings.
target_audience: English-speaking US general audience interested in law, policing, everyday rights, and how systems work; maximally relatable because nearly everyone drives
demand_evidence: 'Can the police search my car / know your rights at a traffic stop' is one of the highest-volume everyday-law queries on YouTube and search; this case line is the legal floor under all of it.

This channel's own analytics (2026-07-04) show its top-retained videos are second-person Fourth-Amendment 'can the police do X to you' explainers (phone search, stop-and-frisk, phone tracking). Car search is the largest untapped topic in that exact vein.
Landmark-case explainers sustain durable long-tail search interest.
competition: Most existing videos either give quick 'know your rights' tips or argue traffic-stop politics; few center the neutral causal story of how the automobile exception was built in 1925 and precisely limited in 2018.
differentiation: Frames the everyday roadside search as a century-old 'hidden system' (Carroll, 1925), present-tense and self-relevant, then pays off the second-person hook with the clean bright line of Collins v. Virginia (2018): the home's curtilage protects even your car. Primary-source citations, neutral advertiser-safe tone. Flagship 'revolution' build targeting the north-star metrics (CTR 6%+, APV 45%+, 30s retention 70%+).
research_feasibility: High: all anchor opinions are public and authoritative — Carroll v. United States, 267 U.S. 132 (1925); Collins v. Virginia, 584 U.S. ___ (2018); Arizona v. Gant, 556 U.S. 332 (2009); Byrd v. United States (2018); scope cases Ross (1982) and Acevedo (1991). Cornell LII and Oyez provide full opinions, syllabi and oral-argument records.
visual_feasibility: High: roadside stop reconstruction, an animated diagram of a car's searchable zones vs the protected curtilage of a home, a motorcycle under a tarp in a driveway, probable-cause-vs-hunch contrast, a 1925->2018 timeline, all with anonymous figures (no real-person likeness).
risk_notes: Landmark + recent decided cases; opinions are public domain / official - advertiser-friendly.
Policing topic: keep strictly neutral (neither anti- nor pro-police). Present the automobile exception and its limits as settled law, not accusation.

Collins v. Virginia (2018) involves living people (Ryan Collins; the officer). Describe strictly by role and accurately as to the record; NO real-person likeness in AI visuals (invariant 11); no defamation.
Do NOT state jurisdiction-specific practices (e.g., the evolving status of the smell of marijuana) as a blanket national rule; flag as state-dependent.
Generated visuals are illustration/reconstruction, never presented as authentic footage.
kill_conditions: Cannot source the automobile-exception holding (Carroll) and the curtilage limit (Collins) to the primary opinions plus one independent authoritative reference.
